reviews.reasoning: This is the best-evidenced span in Psalm 147 and I confirm it from bytes: the second-person feminine suffixed forms are confined to exactly these three verses — אֱלֹהַ֣יִךְ (oshb:Ps.147.12); שְׁעָרָ֑יִךְ, בָּנַ֣יִךְ, בְּקִרְבֵּֽךְ (oshb:Ps.147.13); גְּבוּלֵ֥ךְ, יַשְׂבִּיעֵֽךְ (oshb:Ps.147.14) — 6 tokens over 3 verses, all byte tier, with none in MT 147:1-11 or 147:15-20 (the two other final-kaf tokens in the psalm, בֵּרַ֖ךְ at oshb:Ps.147.13 and מַשְׁלִ֣יךְ at oshb:Ps.147.17, are root-final, not suffixes). The opening quote reaches byte tier and WEB “Praise Yahweh, Jerusalem! Praise your God, Zion!” (web:Ps.147.12) is verbatim. The Jerusalem echo is real and, correctly, disclosed as a cross-seam device: the place-name occurs in exactly 2 verses of Psalm 147 (MT 147:2 and 147:12, skeleton tier). The defect is a false characterization of the rest of the psalm in the same signal.

challenges.claim: observed_substrate_signals[0] characterizes the remainder of Psalm 147 as 'third-person description or first-person-plural summons'; Psalm 147 contains no first-person-plural summons at all, and its other summonses are second-person imperatives, so the contrast that carries the row's opening warrant is misstated.
challenges.evidence: Enumerating every first-person-plural exponent in Psalm 147 from the bytes: the tokens ending in the 1cp element are 4 tokens over 3 verses (skeleton tier) — אֱלֹהֵ֑ינוּ (oshb:Ps.147.1), אֲדוֹנֵ֣ינוּ (oshb:Ps.147.5), לֵאלֹהֵ֣ינוּ (oshb:Ps.147.7), all nouns with the 1cp pronominal suffix, which WEB renders “our God” (web:Ps.147.1), “our Lord” (web:Ps.147.5) and “our God” (web:Ps.147.7); the fourth, עֱנ֣וּ (oshb:Ps.147.7), is the second-person plural imperative WEB renders “Sing to Yahweh with thanksgiving.” (web:Ps.147.7). No 1cp prefix-conjugation verb exists in the psalm either: the only nun-initial tokens are 4 tokens over 3 verses — נָ֝עִים and נָאוָ֥ה (oshb:Ps.147.1), נִדְחֵ֖י (oshb:Ps.147.2), נוֹתֵ֣ן (oshb:Ps.147.9) — two adjectives, a construct noun and a participle, none a 1cp imperfect. The psalm's other summonses are second-person imperatives: הַ֥לְלוּ (oshb:Ps.147.1) and עֱנ֣וּ / זַמְּר֖וּ (oshb:Ps.147.7), all byte tier. check_universals.py flags the same signal (path [2].observed_substrate_signals[0]). The fact that is genuinely proprietary to this span is the ADDRESSEE, not the mood: the 2fs suffix run confined to MT 147:12-14 (6 tokens over 3 verses, byte tier, enumerated in this review's reasoning field).

reviews.reasoning: Every load-bearing claim re-derives. Psalm 148 is an identity psalm (web_mt_offset_map.json rule identity, 14 = 14), so no dual-cite arithmetic is owed. All four Hebrew quotes reach byte tier under collate.py and all WEB quotations are verbatim. The panel opener is byte-true (מִן הָאָ֑רֶץ at oshb:Ps.148.7 answering מִן הַשָּׁמַ֑יִם at oshb:Ps.148.1), the closing frame claim is inventory-true (Ps.148.14 under verse_final, Ps.148.1 under verse_initial) and byte-true, and the row makes no selah, paseq, inverted-nun, suspended-letter or K/Q claim to check against the inventories — pmarks_Ps.json shows 0 selah verses and 0 K/Q notes in MT 148:7-14, while the 2 paseq segs that do fall in the span (MT 148:13, 148:14; seg layer, single-witness) are never boundary evidence and the row correctly does not lean on them. The rejected_alternative is single-sentence and argues the right object — the purpose-clause echo binds catalog to close. I re-derived that echo token by token: of the four tokens of the formula, 4 of 4 match at skeleton tier, 3 of 4 at accent_stripped tier, and exactly 1 of 4 — the object marker אֶת (oshb:Ps.148.5, standing identically at oshb:Ps.148.13) — is byte-identical between the two verses; the two verbs differ even accent-stripped. Observation recorded without filing: 'almost token for token, byte-checked' is true as a process statement (both quotes are byte-true to their own verses) but does not name the tier at which the IDENTITY holds, which is skeleton (4 of 4 tokens); naming it would satisfy the campaign's tier discipline without weakening the argument, since the echo is genuinely exact consonantally.

The seam at 149:4|5 is defensible and the row's honesty about it is good: the grounding clause closes the summons, the setting changes at MT 149:5, and the row discloses the term that straddles its own seam and holds confidence at medium instead of high. The frame claim is inventory-true (Ps.149.1 verse_initial, Ps.149.9 verse_final), Psalm 149 is an identity psalm (9 = 9) so no dual-cite arithmetic is owed, the WEB quotations are verbatim, and the two-row division tiles the psalm exactly. But two of the row's three Hebrew quotes are not byte-true to the staged source, and the sweep citation is written in the book-wide format while carrying a psalm-scoped figure. Fidelity note for the author wave, not filed: WEB renders MT 149:1's frame opener “Praise Yahweh!” (web:Ps.149.1) whereas it renders the same Hebrew “Praise Yah!” (web:Ps.149.9) at the frame's close and at MT 147:1, 147:20, 148:1 and 148:14 — the two halves of this psalm's frame therefore appear in different English on this row and its partner, which is WEB's divergence and worth one clause of disclosure.

Of those, Psalm 149 accounts for exactly 3 (MT 149:1, 149:5, 149:9) — the row's intended figure — and the immediately preceding psalm carries the same term at MT 148:14, where the closing phrase לְכָל חֲסִידָ֗יו (oshb:Ps.149.9) is byte-distinct from that verse's meteg-bearing form. The same wording appears twice on this row (rationale signal and device_notes) and once on the 149:5-9 row, so the cure is one edit installed across all three occurrences.
